extracted.intended_audience: New and experienced NIH grant peer reviewers / study section members
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for scientists serving as reviewers on NIH/CSR study sections about how to read applications, write critiques, participate in meetings, and score fairly and constructively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start early and manage workload
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t be overwhelmed by the number of applications. Just start reading as soon as you get your application assignments. Give each application adequate time for a full and comprehensive review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get started right away to discover if you have a conflict with an application. It is cumbersome to reassign the application late in the game. You want to make sure every application gets due diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify conflicts of interest promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Get started right away to discover if you have a conflict with an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovering conflicts early avoids cumbersome late reassignments and ensures every application receives due diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult your Scientific Review Officer (SRO) when uncertain
rubrics_metrics.description: You can clarify any uncertainties about the review process with your scientific review officer (SRO) prior to writing your reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parts of the review process or your role are unclear, ask the SRO so your written review and meeting participation are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain opinions objectively, not just state them
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t just express your opinions: Be prepared to explain your opinion as objectively as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support judgments with reasons and evidence from the application so others can understand and evaluate your viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call out fatal flaws clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t mince words: If you feel there is an immutable and fatal flaw, say so in your review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit when a problem is fundamental (the analogy used: 'resubmit the Titanic' otherwise). Clear statements about fatal flaws help programmatic decisions and prevent unnecessary resubmissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t be too critical: An application doesn’t have to be totally perfect for you to give it a good score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some reviewers habitually criticize; avoid undue harshness and weigh both negatives and positives when scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a balanced assessment: strengths and weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Paint a big and balanced picture: ... You need to say what the strengths are and explain the big picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inexperienced reviewers often focus on weaknesses. State both strengths and weaknesses and place the project in the broader context so the committee can judge relative merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect applicants and their efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are just like you: They are excited about the science and often it is their life’s work. You really want to respect that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be professional and considerate in tone; recognize the effort applicants put into proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for page/format constraints when judging detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that applicants can’t provide all the details in the shorter NIH format. Consider if the PI has sufficient command of the material to make it likely the project will succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate PI competence and feasibility even when detailed methods or data are absent due to format limits; avoid penalizing missing minutiae that are unreasonable to expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rewrite the application or act as a mentor
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t try to rewrite an application: You are a critic, not a mentor. Your comments should be generous when possible and polite at all times. They should be clear enough that an investigator has a sense of what needs to be done in order to craft a more competitive application if the current version is unfunded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not suggest better methodologies or designs, or provide salient references. Provide feedback sufficient to guide revision but avoid prescriptive rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score the application, not your discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Score the application, not your discipline: Try not to root for work in your own field, and don’t inflate your score because you think there isn’t enough funding going into an area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bias toward your own specialty or advocacy for funding distribution; judge the merits of the application itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep written comments calibrated to the score
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep your reviews in sync: Make sure that your comments and what you say are calibrated to the score that you’re giving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistency between the narrative critique (strengths/weaknesses) and the numeric score so reviewers and program staff have a coherent record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare notes so you can speak efficiently
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare the notes for your assigned applications well: So you can be conversational and efficient at your meeting. You don’t want to read your critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-prepared notes let you present succinctly and respond to discussion without reading long passages, preserving study section time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the group nature of peer review and your limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember you’re not expected to know everything: Peer review is a group process with multiple individuals providing special expertise and different points of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on the combined expertise of the panel; if you feel unqualified to evaluate aspects, alert the SRO so they can ensure appropriate review coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about what will be learned and uncertain areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Be very clear about the strengths or the weaknesses and try to give a sense of what you think will be learned by things ... And don’t be afraid to say there was a part of an application you didn’t really understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State expected knowledge gains/outcomes and be candid about unclear parts rather than guessing; flag unclear areas for discussion or SRO action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus oral presentations on score-relevant issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk about what matters: Oral presentations at study section ... should focus on issues that help people arrive at a score. ... Just focus on the major strengths and weaknesses. Limit your description of the research and don’t try to enumerate every minor flaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid lengthy background or exhaustive lists of minor problems; concentrate the discussion on the few points that affect the assessment and scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide relevant historical context for resubmissions and renewals
rubrics_metrics.description: Give key historical facts: If you are reviewing a resubmitted application, let us know if the investigators were responsive to the initial review group. If you are reviewing a renewal proposal for continued funding, please comment on the progress the investigators made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefly report responsiveness to prior reviews for resubmissions and concrete progress for renewals to inform the panel about trajectory and improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rehashing prior presenters; add value
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t rehash: If you agree with everything the previous reviewer said, say so and then say what you see as different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not repeat prior presentations verbatim; highlight differences in perspective or additional points so panel time is efficient and non-redundant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on evaluating the application, not self-promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on the applications: Always remember that the study section is about the applicants, and not about you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using your presentation as an opportunity to show how smart you are; stay applicant-centric and decision-focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate significance and transformative potential (big picture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on the big picture and not the little details. Is the application transformative? Or does the proposed research address an important need, even if it is not necessarily transformative?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess overall potential impact, importance of the problem addressed, and whether the project advances the field, beyond minor technical details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be confident in your expertise but open to changing your mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t be unsettled if someone disagrees with you ... Don’t be intimidated by a senior reviewer who comes down on an application you feel is terrific ... Be flexible: Listen and be open to changing your mind if new and compelling perspectives come to the table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State your informed opinion clearly; engage constructively with dissenting views and be willing to revise judgments when persuaded by evidence or argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage professionally, build networks, and learn from the process
rubrics_metrics.description: Meet new friends and colleagues ... Enjoy the experience: You have the opportunity to see firsthand cutting-edge science ... and you’re going to become a better grant writer as a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach review as both a service and a professional development opportunity—network, learn about emerging work, and improve your own grant-writing through exposure to other proposals.
